title: Turning Experience Into Strong Evidence
summary: Learn how to turn projects, schoolwork, volunteering, training, teamwork, and other experiences into clear examples of what you contributed, learned, produced, and can support with evidence.
objectives: Identify useful evidence from school, projects, training, volunteering, and work experiences.
Describe personal contributions without taking credit for other people's work.
Connect an experience to a relevant skill or employer expectation without overstating mastery.

vocab.def: A piece of work that helps show what a person produced, contributed, or practiced.
The specific part of a project, task, or result that a person was responsible for.
Information about where a piece of work came from and how it was created.
A statement about experience or ability that is supported by appropriate examples or records.

sections.heading: Experience can come from more than paid employment
sections.body: Projects, classes, volunteering, community work, clubs, simulations, internships, supervised practice, and personal projects can all provide useful examples when they are described accurately.

sections.heading: Describe your contribution
sections.body: When work was completed by a team, explain what you specifically planned, built, tested, documented, researched, presented, organized, or improved.

sections.heading: Connect examples to the opportunity
sections.body: The strongest examples are relevant to the employer or opportunity. A project may demonstrate communication, problem solving, teamwork, reliability, digital skills, safety awareness, or another useful capability.

sections.heading: Evidence should stay truthful
sections.body: A work sample or project can support what you actually demonstrated, but it should not be used to claim a credential, job title, verified competency, or professional qualification that has not been established.

practice.prompt: A five-person team built a website and you tested accessibility and documented defects. How should you describe your contribution?
practice.answer: State that you performed accessibility testing and documented defects rather than claiming you built the entire website.

practice.prompt: You completed a simulated workplace project. Can you describe it as professional employment?
practice.answer: No. Describe it accurately as a simulation, project, training activity, or supervised learning experience.

quiz.question: Which statement best demonstrates evidence-based professional presentation?
options: Describe your actual contribution and connect it to a relevant example
Claim ownership of an entire team project
Turn a simulation into professional employment
Claim a credential because you practiced related skills
quiz.answer: Describe your actual contribution and connect it to a relevant example

lab.objective: Select three simulated or learner-chosen experiences and turn each into a short evidence-based description covering context, personal contribution, result, and what the example demonstrates.

reflectionPrompt: Which experience from your life could become a strong professional example if you described your contribution more clearly?
